unit.title: How agents work: the loop, tools and memory

lesson.title: How it picks a tool
lesson.subtitle: The tools line, the arguments, and the slips a model makes

video.title: How it picks a tool
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: A list: My request; A wrong copy; How it chooses.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: I asked an agent to explain the term malware. It looked up “the term malware”, not “malware”! So how does a model choose a tool, and why does it slip?

scenes.animation: The Darsi mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how an agent picks a tool, and fills in the details.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Before your request, the app writes a tools line: the names of the tools that are on. The model reads that line and your words, and nothing else. From them, it picks one tool, or none.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: reminder{"text":"collect the homework", …
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Each tool needs details, like a place and a day. The model copies them from your words into the call, so Kafi stays Kafi. Days and times go in a fixed form that the tool can read.

scenes.visual: A list: weather: a place and a day; reminder: its text and a time; One missing? It should ask.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The details in a call are called its arguments. Each tool has its own: the weather needs a place and a day, a reminder needs its text and a time. When one is missing, a good agent asks.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: How good is Darsi Tiny? With wordings it was trained on, it gets the tool and every argument right ninety-six to ninety-eight times in a hundred. With new wordings, about seventy-eight to eighty. That’s roughly one slip in five.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Why does a new way of asking make Darsi Tiny slip more often?

scenes.visual: A list: Learned patterns of wording; A new form fits less well; Big models: fewer slips, not none.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: It learned patterns of wording. A small model has seen each kind of request in a few dozen forms, and a new form fits them less well. Big models have seen far more, so they slip less, but they still slip.

scenes.visual: A list: “the term malware”; 9Z copied as 9C; France: the glossary, not “I can’t”.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Here are real slips from the lab. Asked about class 9Z, which doesn’t exist, it wrote 9C, a class it knows. And the capital of France, asked one way, sent it to the glossary instead of saying it can’t.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: So the app checks every call
scenes.narration: So the app checks every call before it runs. Is the tool on? Did each name come from your words? Is the time a real time? A few lines of code catch these slips.

scenes.visual: A list: Weather off: what now?; 9Z: read the check; France, asked two ways.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: how an agent picks a tool
scenes.narration: In the app, switch the weather tool off and ask about it. Ask what 9Z has tomorrow, and read the check under the call. Then ask about France, in two ways.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Your turn. I asked for a reminder at eight, and the call says nine. What should the app do?

scenes.visual: Summary points: The tools line and your words; Copied details; new wordings slip; The app checks every call.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: The tools line and your words · Copied details; new wordings slip · The app checks every call
scenes.narration: Stop it, and ask me again: nine isn’t what I said. Remember: the model reads the tools line and your words. It copies details into arguments, and new wordings slip more. So the app checks every call.

scenes.visual: A list: One pupil plays the agent; A card of request patterns; Same request, five wordings; Which wordings slip?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: one pupil plays the agent, with a card of request patterns. Classmates ask for the same thing in five ways. Which wordings make the agent slip?

checkpoints.prompt: Why does a new way of asking make Darsi Tiny slip more often?

options.text: It learned patterns of wording, and a new wording fits them less well
It needs more time to think about new wordings
Its tools change when the wording changes

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it learned patterns from the wordings in its training, so a new wording fits them less well: 96–98% right falls to about 78–80%.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — its tools and its speed don’t change. It learned patterns of wording, and new ones fit them less well.

checkpoints.prompt: You asked for a reminder at eight, and the call says nine. What should the app do?

options.text: Run it: nine is close enough
Stop it, and ask you again
Run it, and fix it later if needed

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — nine never appeared in your words, so the call is a slip. The app should stop it before it runs, and ask you again.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a wrong time means a wrong reminder. Stop the call before it runs, and ask again.
